headline: Highest risk is B data leakage and cascading error: oh-my-openagent has broad networked, browser-enabled, multi-instance support while marker is a local document processor with no filesystem or network access.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: marker has no filesystem read/write, network egress, MCP, or browser surfaces, so it cannot directly ingest oh-my-openagent output by default. The only plausible bridge is manual copy-paste into marker’s document-processing flow, which is unusual and low blast radius. oh-my-openagent can emit content through browser/MCP-driven workflows, but the pair lacks a documented shared channel.
conditions: IF the operator manually copies oh-my-openagent output into marker as trusted document content, prompt injection becomes plausible.
IF a shared filesystem or clipboard bridge is added outside the profiles, the risk increases.
mitigations: Keep the agents on separate workspaces.
Do not paste agent B output into marker without review.
Disable browser-driven content ingestion for the workflow.
Use a human approval step before reusing generated text.
requires-engineering: add provenance tagging between agents.

B_data_leakage.rationale: marker touches no data classes and has no network egress, so it is not a leakage source. oh-my-openagent, however, touches project code, AGENTS.md, README.md, session history, and provider auth data, and has broad network egress plus API calls. If both share a workspace, B can expose A-derived files or secrets to third parties; the pathway exists in common setups, though not proven by direct evidence.
conditions: IF both agents are pointed at the same repository or home directory, B can transmit A-accessible files off-host.
IF provider auth prompts or session history contain secrets, oh-my-openagent may send them to external services.
mitigations: Separate the agents into different directories.
Remove secrets from shared workspaces.
Restrict oh-my-openagent network access where possible.
Review files before opening them in B.
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent workspace isolation.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: marker cannot write files, modify git, or spawn subprocesses, so it cannot contend for mutable resources. oh-my-openagent supports subprocesses, broad network egress, multiple instances, and task-scoped isolation, which can still conflict with shared mutable resources if the operator places both on the same workspace. The overlap is real but asymmetric, so medium is appropriate.
conditions: IF both agents are given write access to the same directory through external tooling, conflicts can occur.
IF oh-my-openagent instances operate on the same mutable project state, race conditions become plausible.
mitigations: Avoid shared writable directories.
Run only one oh-my-openagent instance per project.
Use git branches for any mutable work.
Pause one agent before the other edits the same files.
requires-engineering: add locking around shared resources.

D_cascading_error.rationale: marker is a document-processing agent, so it can plausibly consume oh-my-openagent output as input, but marker has no explicit verification or critique controls in the profile. oh-my-openagent can generate project code, README, and session-history-derived content that may be treated as authoritative downstream. The pair therefore supports an unverified handoff, though not an automated action chain.
conditions: IF marker is used to transform or summarize oh-my-openagent output without human review, errors can cascade.
IF oh-my-openagent produces incorrect code or instructions that marker republishes, downstream consumers may trust them.
mitigations: Insert a human verification step between agents.
Require source citations before marker republishes content.
Limit marker to formatting, not factual synthesis.
Flag uncertain outputs for review.
requires-engineering: add automated consistency checks.

E_compliance.rationale: marker is open-source and locally constrained, while oh-my-openagent explicitly handles provider authentication data, anonymous telemetry, and session history and uses broad network egress. That creates a compliance mismatch around retention and third-party transfer if regulated or sensitive data enters the workflow. The profile does not show a specific residency regime, so I avoid higher severity.
conditions: IF regulated data or secrets are processed through oh-my-openagent, third-party transfer and retention obligations apply.
IF the operator expects local-only handling, B's networked telemetry and provider calls violate that expectation.
mitigations: Do not route regulated data through oh-my-openagent.
Review telemetry and retention settings.
Strip secrets before use.
Document data-handling boundaries.
requires-engineering: add a DPA/residency control layer.
